objectives: Describe volcanism at divergent margins (mid-ocean ridges) and explain why it produces mostly basalt.
Explain convergent-margin subduction volcanism and the origin of the Pacific Ring of Fire.
Contrast plate-boundary volcanism with intraplate hotspots and the Wilson plume hypothesis, and connect each setting to its characteristic magma chemistry.

slides.title: Divergent margins: building crust at the ridges
slides.body:
The theory of **plate tectonics**, assembled in the 1960s from **Alfred Wegener's** earlier idea of continental drift, **Harry Hess's** seafloor-spreading hypothesis, and the magnetic-stripe evidence of **Fred Vine** and **Drummond Matthews**, organizes nearly all of Earth's volcanism into three settings. The first is the **divergent margin**, where two plates pull apart.

The archetype is the **mid-ocean ridge**, a 65,000-km submarine mountain chain that includes the **Mid-Atlantic Ridge** and the **East Pacific Rise**. As plates separate, hot mantle wells up to fill the gap. Because the mantle's solidus rises with pressure, this upwelling drives **decompression melting**: the rising peridotite crosses its solidus simply by losing pressure, with no added heat or water. The result is copious **basaltic** magma — specifically **mid-ocean-ridge basalt (MORB)**, the most voluminous igneous rock on the planet. MORB is low in silica, low in viscosity, and erupts effusively onto the seafloor, where seawater quenches it into characteristic bulbous **pillow lavas**. New oceanic crust is manufactured here continuously; the entire ocean floor is younger than about $200\ \text{Myr}$ because it is constantly created at ridges and destroyed at subduction zones. The newly formed lithosphere cools and subsides as it ages, and its depth below the ridge crest deepens roughly as the square root of crustal age, $d \propto \sqrt{t}$, the classic half-space cooling result.

Most ridge volcanism is hidden beneath kilometers of seawater, but where a ridge rises above sea level we can watch it directly. **Iceland** sits astride the Mid-Atlantic Ridge atop a coincident hotspot, which is why it is so volcanically active; eruptions such as **Laki (1783)**, **Eyjafjallajökull (2010)**, and the **Fagradalsfjall** fissure eruptions of 2021 onward all express divergent-margin and plume basaltic magmatism. Continental rifts capture the same process at an earlier stage: the **East African Rift**, with volcanoes like **Ol Doinyo Lengai** and **Erta Ale**, is a continent in the act of splitting, and its basaltic-to-unusual magmas record decompression melting beneath thinning crust.

The defining feature of divergent volcanism is its chemistry. Because it is fed by decompression melting of dry mantle with little crustal interaction, ridge magma is overwhelmingly **basaltic** and erupts **effusively**. There are no towering Plinian columns at a normal mid-ocean ridge; the silica content is simply too low. This makes divergent margins the quiet, productive workhorses of Earth's volcanic system, and a clean contrast to the explosive arcs we turn to next.

question.question: Mid-ocean ridges produce enormous volumes of basalt. Which melting mechanism is responsible, and why is the magma basaltic rather than rhyolitic?
options: Flux melting; the seawater makes the magma silica-rich
Decompression melting of upwelling mantle; melting dry peridotite at low pressure yields low-silica basalt
Heat-induced crustal melting; the thick ocean crust melts to basalt
Friction melting from the spreading plates
question.explanation: At a divergent margin, plates pull apart and mantle rises to fill the gap. Losing pressure pushes the hot peridotite across its solidus (decompression melting) with no added heat or water. Partial melting of mantle peridotite yields low-silica basaltic magma (MORB), and there is little silica-rich crust to assimilate, so the product is basalt, not rhyolite.

hints: Plates pulling apart means pressure drops on the rising mantle.
What composition comes from partial melting of peridotite?
slides.workedSolution: Spreading lets hot mantle ascend; the pressure drop alone crosses the solidus, which is decompression melting. The source is dry peridotite and there is no thick silica-rich crust to interact with, so partial melting produces basalt (MORB), low in silica and viscosity. Option B is correct.

slides.title: Convergent margins: subduction and the Ring of Fire
slides.body:
The second setting is the **convergent margin**, where plates collide and the denser one — almost always oceanic — sinks beneath the other in a process called **subduction**. As the cold slab descends into the mantle, hydrous minerals in it break down and release water and other volatiles into the overlying **mantle wedge**. This **flux melting**, introduced in the previous lesson, lowers the wedge's solidus and generates magma that rises to build a chain of volcanoes parallel to the trench — a **volcanic arc**.

Subduction volcanoes are the dangerous ones. Their magmas are typically **andesitic to dacitic**, higher in silica and viscosity than ridge basalts, and they carry abundant dissolved water. High viscosity plus high gas content is precisely the recipe for explosive, **Plinian** eruptions. The world's great composite cones — **stratovolcanoes** — are subduction products: **Mount Fuji** in Japan, **Mount Rainier** and **Mount St. Helens** in the Cascades of the United States, **Mount Pinatubo** in the Philippines, **Krakatoa** and **Tambora** in Indonesia, and the long chain of the **Andes** in South America.

Most of these encircle one ocean. The **Pacific Ring of Fire** is the roughly 40,000-km belt of subduction zones rimming the Pacific basin, home to about three-quarters of the world's active and dormant subaerial volcanoes and the great majority of large explosive eruptions and megathrust earthquakes. The Ring of Fire is not a coincidence; it is the surface expression of the Pacific Plate and surrounding oceanic plates being consumed at trenches such as the **Mariana Trench**, the **Japan Trench**, and the **Peru-Chile Trench**.

The geometry of an arc carries information. Magma is generated where the slab reaches a critical depth (commonly $\approx 100\ \text{km}$), so the line of volcanoes — the **volcanic front** — sits a predictable distance inland from the trench, set by the slab's dip. To first order the horizontal trench-to-arc distance is $x \approx h/\tan\theta$, where $h$ is the critical generation depth and $\theta$ is the slab dip, so steeper slabs ($\theta$ large) place the arc closer to the trench. A steeply dipping slab gives a narrow arc close to the trench; a shallow slab gives a broad arc far inland, and in extreme cases of **flat-slab subduction** (as beneath parts of the central Andes) the volcanic gap widens or volcanism shuts off entirely. Behind some arcs, the overriding plate stretches and opens a **back-arc basin** with its own spreading and basaltic volcanism. Reading arc geometry, magma chemistry, and trench position together lets a geologist infer the configuration of a subduction zone that may lie tens of kilometers underground.

question.question: Roughly what fraction of the world's subaerial active volcanoes lie within the Pacific Ring of Fire? Express it as a percentage (a value near three-quarters is expected).
question.hint: The Ring of Fire hosts roughly three out of every four of the world's land volcanoes.

slides.title: Hotspots and the Wilson plume hypothesis
slides.body:
Most volcanoes sit on plate boundaries, but a striking minority erupt in the middle of plates, thousands of kilometers from any ridge or trench. The classic example is **Hawaii**, a chain of volcanic islands in the heart of the Pacific Plate. To explain such **intraplate** volcanism, the Canadian geophysicist **J. Tuzo Wilson** proposed in **1963** that a fixed, deep-seated source of heat — a **hotspot**, fed by a narrow **mantle plume** rising from deep in the mantle — melts the base of a plate that drifts overhead. As the plate moves over the stationary plume, the volcano is carried away and goes extinct while a new one forms above the hotspot, producing a **time-progressive chain** of volcanoes that gets older with distance from the active center. This is the **Wilson plume hypothesis** (later elaborated by **W. Jason Morgan** in 1971).

Hawaii is the textbook confirmation. The active volcanoes **Kīlauea** and **Mauna Loa** sit at the southeast end of the chain over the present hotspot, while islands grow progressively older to the northwest. The chain continues as the drowned **Emperor Seamounts**, and the sharp **bend** between the Hawaiian and Emperor segments — dated to about **47 million years ago** — records a change in Pacific Plate motion (and possibly some plume motion). Other proposed hotspots include **Yellowstone** beneath the North American continent, **Iceland** (a plume coincident with a ridge), **Réunion** in the Indian Ocean, and the **Galápagos**.

The magma chemistry of hotspots reflects their origin. Like ridges, plumes melt by **decompression** of hot upwelling mantle, so oceanic hotspots erupt mainly fluid **basalt** — the gentle lava fountains and pāhoehoe flows that make Kīlauea so approachable to scientists. This basalt, called **ocean-island basalt (OIB)**, differs subtly in trace-element and isotopic signature from MORB, hinting that plumes sample deeper, more primitive or recycled mantle. But where a plume sits beneath thick **continental** crust, as at **Yellowstone**, the basaltic heat input drives crustal melting (heat-induced melting) and generates large volumes of explosive **rhyolite** — which is why Yellowstone, despite being a hotspot, has produced caldera-forming supereruptions rather than gentle Hawaiian flows.

So the same plume produces wildly different volcanoes depending on what lies above it, underscoring the central lesson of this unit: **tectonic setting plus crustal context controls magma chemistry, and magma chemistry controls eruption style.** Three settings, three dominant compositions — divergent and oceanic-hotspot basalt by decompression, arc andesite by flux melting, continental-hotspot rhyolite by heat-induced melting — and from those compositions everything about how a volcano behaves can be inferred.

question.question: The Hawaiian-Emperor seamount chain becomes progressively older with distance from Kīlauea. According to the Wilson plume hypothesis, what does this age progression demonstrate?
options: The mantle plume migrates rapidly across the Pacific
A roughly fixed hotspot melts the base of the Pacific Plate, which drifts overhead, so successive volcanoes are carried away and a chain forms
Each island erupted simultaneously and then eroded at different rates
Subduction created the islands one after another
question.explanation: Wilson proposed a relatively stationary deep hotspot. As the overriding Pacific Plate moves, each volcano is rafted off the hotspot and goes extinct while a new one forms above the plume. The result is a time-progressive chain that ages away from the active center (Kīlauea), exactly the Hawaiian-Emperor pattern. The Hawaiian-Emperor bend at ~47 Ma records a change in plate motion.

hints: The hotspot is roughly fixed; what is moving?
Older volcanoes are farther from the active vent.
slides.workedSolution: A fixed plume plus a moving plate naturally makes a conveyor-belt chain: the volcano above the hotspot is active, then drifts off and dies as the plate carries it along, while a new volcano ignites over the plume. Ages therefore increase with distance from Kīlauea, which is the observed Hawaiian-Emperor progression. Option B is correct.

question.question: Identifying a volcano's tectonic setting
question.prompt: You are handed three volcanoes with no location labels. Volcano X erupts fluid basalt as submarine pillow lavas along a long linear ridge. Volcano Y is a steep andesitic cone that produces violent ash columns and sits in a chain parallel to a deep ocean trench. Volcano Z erupts fluid basalt but sits alone in the middle of an oceanic plate at the young end of an age-progressive island chain. Assign each volcano to its tectonic setting (divergent margin, convergent/subduction margin, or intraplate hotspot) and justify each call from the evidence given.

slides.title: One framework, three signatures
slides.body:
Plate tectonics gives volcanology its global organizing principle. Almost every volcano on Earth can be assigned to one of three settings, and each setting writes a distinctive chemical signature into its magma:
- **Divergent margins** (mid-ocean ridges; continental rifts like the **East African Rift**). Melting by **decompression** of upwelling mantle yields voluminous low-silica **MORB**. Eruptions are effusive; the **Mid-Atlantic Ridge** and **Iceland** are the type localities.
- **Convergent margins** (subduction zones forming the **Pacific Ring of Fire**). Melting by **flux** as the slab dehydrates yields wetter, higher-silica **andesite and dacite**. Eruptions are explosive; **Mount Fuji**, **Mount Rainier**, **Pinatubo**, **Krakatoa**, and the **Andes** are the type localities.
- **Intraplate hotspots** (**Hawaii**, **Yellowstone**, **Réunion**, the **Galápagos**). Melting by **decompression** above a deep **mantle plume** (the **Wilson hypothesis**, 1963). Over oceanic plates the product is fluid **OIB** basalt (**Kīlauea**); over thick continental crust, heat-induced crustal melting yields explosive **rhyolite** (**Yellowstone**).

Two deeper lessons emerge. First, **the melting mechanism predicts the chemistry, and the chemistry predicts the behavior.** Decompression and dry mantle give effusive basalt; flux melting gives gas-rich, viscous, explosive arc magma; heat-induced crustal melting gives the most silicic and explosive products of all. This is the same silica-viscosity-volatile logic from Lessons 1 and 2, now anchored to where on the planet a volcano sits.

Second, **context can override the source.** Hawaii and Yellowstone are both hotspots, yet one builds gentle shields and the other has produced VEI 8 caldera eruptions, purely because of the crust they sit beneath. A volcanologist who knows only the tectonic setting can make a good first guess about eruption style; one who also knows the crustal context and the degree of differentiation can do far better.

With the global framework in place — *where* magma forms and *why* its chemistry differs from setting to setting — we are ready to examine *how* it actually erupts. The next lesson catalogs eruption styles and their products: the difference between **pāhoehoe** and **ʻaʻā** lava, the architecture of an **eruption column**, and the deadly suite of explosive products — **tephra**, **pyroclastic density currents**, and **lahars** — that the silica-rich magmas of subduction zones unleash.
